title: Neuralink Sets 11.32 bps BCI Record Using New Foundation Model
summary:
A dataset of more than 50,000 hours of recorded implant use provided the basis for a new system to stabilize intracortical brain signals. Neuralink used this data to pretrain a brain-computer interface foundation model using self-supervised neural encoders to convert noisy spikes into stable representations. The resulting technology enables "teleporting cursors" that jump directly to targets and has achieved a control speed of 11.32 bits per second, which the company says outperforms most able-bodied people.

The updated decoders maintain functionality for weeks instead of days, reducing calibration requirements for some users from 10 min/day to 10 min/week. Future development goals include creating an API for the motor cortex and pooling data across different trial participants to enable zero-shot or one-shot calibration.

selectedTweets.text:
Our clinical trial participants have now used their Neuralink implants for over 50,000 hours, building one of the largest datasets of intracortical neural activity ever.

We used it to pretrain a foundation model for BCI: self-supervised neural encoders that turn noisy, drifting spikes into stable representations.

Some initial results:
• Decoders that keep working for weeks instead of days. For some users, calibration dropped from 10 min/day to 10 min/week
• Teleporting cursors that jump straight to the intended target
• A new cursor-control record of 11.32 bits per second (exceeding the performance of most able-bodied people)

We’re just getting started. Future directions include pooling data across participants, one-shot (or zero-shot) calibration, and an API for the motor cortex.
